summary: Specifies a new MIKEY General Extension payload to carry the short-term key message and long-term key message payloads defined by the Open Mobile Alliance's BCAST service and content protection specification. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 5410 and RFC 6309.

plainLanguage.summary: Phones that receive broadcast TV need keys to unlock it. This note shows how to deliver those keys inside an existing key-sharing system.

questions: what is the mikey general extension payload
how does mikey carry oma bcast keys
subtitle: Extend MIKEY to carry broadcast TV key management parameters for mobile devices.

tldr.problem: Mobile broadcast services like TV need to deliver content protection keys to receivers, but existing key distribution mechanisms do not support the service-specific attributes required by the Open Mobile Alliance broadcast specification.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a new General Extension payload type (Type 5) for the MIKEY key agreement protocol that can carry OMA broadcast short-term and long-term key messages, allowing the protocol to transport both the key management parameters and the service protection attributes.
tldr.outcome: Broadcast receivers can now obtain both keys and necessary service protection information through a single MIKEY exchange, enabling broadcast content protection to work on mobile devices. Later RFCs (5410, 6309) superseded this specification.

today: RFC 5410 and RFC 6309 supersede this document with updated specifications for MIKEY broadcast key management.

sections.title: Extending MIKEY for Broadcast
sections.content:
MIKEY is a key agreement and key transport protocol that defines a General Extension payload to allow extensions without needing a new protocol. MIKEY is used in mobile networks, including 3GPP broadcast services and the Open Mobile Alliance's broadcast specifications. The OMA BCAST Service and Content Protection specification defines two payloads: the Short-Term Key Message (STKM) and the Long-Term Key Message (LTKM), which carry service protection attributes. These payloads need to be transported in MIKEY messages.

This document specifies how to carry STKM and LTKM payloads inside a MIKEY General Extension payload, allowing broadcast receivers to obtain the necessary key material and service protection information in a single key distribution exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY is how phones get secret keys. OMA BCAST is how broadcast TV works. This document shows how to put broadcast TV key information into MIKEY messages.

sections.title: The General Extension Mechanism
sections.content:
RFC 3830 (the MIKEY specification) defines a General Extension payload that can be used in any MIKEY message to carry arbitrary extension data. The General Extension payload is part of the authenticated or signed data in MIKEY messages, meaning it is integrity protected. Each General Extension carries an 8-bit Type field that identifies the extension type, and a variable-length Data field containing the extension-specific content.

This RFC specifies the use of General Extension Type 5 for OMA BCAST service and content protection. Type 5 carries a Subtype field (8 bits) that distinguishes between different payloads. The LTKM (long-term key message) is subtype 1, and the STKM (short-term key message) is subtype 2. The remainder of the extension is subtype-specific data as defined in the OMA specification. This allows a single MIKEY extension to carry either LTKM or STKM payloads depending on the subtype value.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY has a slot for extra information. This takes that slot (number 5) and puts broadcast key info inside using subtypes: 1 for long-term keys, 2 for short-term keys.

sections.title: Broadcast Key Management and Protection
sections.content:
The LTKM and STKM payloads defined in the OMA BCAST specification carry attributes related to service and content protection, such as encryption algorithms, authentication methods, and key usage policies. Note that the actual encryption keys themselves are not carried in the General Extension payload. Keys are instead encrypted and transported in the MIKEY KEMAC payload, which provides confidentiality for sensitive key material.

When a broadcast receiver initiates a MIKEY key exchange to obtain broadcast content protection keys, the server can include a General Extension payload (Type 5) containing either an LTKM or STKM subtype. The receiver extracts the protection attributes from the extension and the encrypted keys from the KEMAC payload. The MIKEY message provides both authentication of the key material and replay protection, ensuring the broadcast receiver obtains legitimate, non-replayed key information for accessing protected content.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension carries rules like "use this encryption" and "check this way." The actual keys go elsewhere, encrypted. Together they tell the phone how to decrypt the broadcast.

sections.title: Security and Interoperability
sections.content: The General Extension payload is always part of the authenticated or signed data in MIKEY messages, so the LTKM and STKM parameters carried in the extension are always integrity protected. Keys or confidential data MUST NOT be included in the General Extension payload itself; any secret material must be encrypted separately. The specification requires that the General Extension payload be integrity protected and that replay protection, which MIKEY provides, covers the extension as well. Interoperability is ensured through the IANA registry, which manages the assignment of General Extension types and subtypes. OMA BCAST 1.0 implementations must comply with the assignment of Type 5 and subtypes 1 and 2 defined in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The information in the extension is always checked to make sure it has not been tampered with. Secret keys never go in the extension—they go elsewhere, encrypted. Phones and servers that follow this spec will work together.
